text: Cities where a nation's grain and supplies were stored. The Israelites were forced to build them like slaves.
Women who helped mothers give birth, much like midwives today.
A sticky black substance found in the ground (asphalt). It was smeared on baskets and boats to keep water out.
A person who offered sacrifices to God, prayed for the people, and taught the law.
The chief of the priests. Aaron was the first, and his sons succeeded him.
A low, thorny shrub that grows in the wilderness. God called Moses from the flames of such a bush.
An astonishing act showing that God is present. More than a simple miracle, it is a marker that points to something.
A sacred holiday kept at an appointed time to remember God, such as Passover or the Feast of Tabernacles.
Men at Pharaoh's court who practiced secret arts. They imitated the first few plagues but soon gave up.
Meaning 'passing over', Israel's first festival. It remembers the night the plague passed over the houses marked with a lamb's blood.
A small plant that grows between rocks. Tied in a bunch, it was used to dip and sprinkle blood or water.
The beam across the top of a doorway. On Passover night, lamb's blood was put on it and on the two doorposts.
Bread made without yeast, which makes dough rise. Leaving in haste, Israel ate bread without yeast, and this led to the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
Grown men old enough to go to war. Women and children were not included in this count.
Horse-drawn war carts, the most fearsome weapons of the time.
A small hand drum. Women played it and danced on joyful days.
A person who receives God's word and passes it on to others; not merely someone who predicts the future.
Laws and rules God set for his people to keep.
A dry measure of about two liters, the amount of manna one person ate in a day.
The food God gave every day in the wilderness. Its name comes from the question 'What is it?'
The seventh day, when people stop work, rest, and remember God. It runs from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday.
Older leaders who represented their families and tribes, discussing and deciding the people's affairs together.
A raised platform of stones or earth for offering sacrifices; a place for worshiping God.
A sacrifice burned whole on the altar, expressing complete devotion to God.
Animals killed as offerings to God.
An offering celebrating peace between God and people. Part of the meat was shared and eaten together.
Quarrels brought before someone to decide who is right, much like court cases today.
A binding promise God made with his people: he would be their God, and they would be his people.
Washing the body and clothes to come before God. Outward cleanness showed that the heart was being prepared.
The figure of a god carved from wood, stone, or metal. Such things made to be worshiped are called idols.
Sexual relations between a married person and someone other than their spouse.
A blue gemstone, thought to be sapphire or lapis lazuli.
The two stone tablets on which God engraved the Ten Commandments. They were later kept inside the ark of the covenant.
A tent sanctuary set up and moved through the wilderness, a sign that God lived among his people.
The tent where God met with Moses and the people; another name for the tabernacle.
The stone tablets engraved with the Ten Commandments, so called because they bore witness to the covenant between God and his people.
A wooden chest covered with gold that held the stone tablets. It showed that God was among his people, and the priests carried it.
The gold lid on the ark of the covenant. Each year the high priest sprinkled blood on it to cleanse the people's sins.
A heavy cloth dividing a space. In the tabernacle it screened off the most holy place.
The table in the tabernacle where twelve loaves of bread were always set out before God.
A gold lampstand with seven branches of lights that always lit the inside of the tabernacle.
A small gold altar in the tabernacle where incense was burned every morning and evening.
The large bronze altar in the tabernacle courtyard, where animals were burned as sacrifices.
A large bronze basin where the priests washed their hands and feet.
The length from the elbow to the fingertips, about 45 centimeters.
The distance a person can walk in a day, about 30 kilometers.
People who slip secretly into enemy land to see how things are and report back.
One of the large clans descended from the twelve sons of Jacob. Israel was made up of twelve tribes.
A pan holding burning coals for offering incense. Only priests could use one before God.
A terrible disease that spreads among people.
A snake made of bronze. Whoever looked at it lived, and Jesus compared his own cross to it.
Money or goods paid for fortune-telling or for pronouncing blessings and curses.
People who held high positions in the government.
The teaching and commandments God gave through Moses. The Book of the Law is the book where they were written.
The posts standing on either side of a door.
The stalks of the flax plant, used to weave linen. They were laid out on roofs to dry.
A shallow place where a river can be crossed, or a landing place for boats.
A rite in which the foreskin of a boy was cut, a sign of the covenant marking God's people.
Here, the shofar, a trumpet made from a ram's horn. It was blown at festivals, in battle, and to announce great events.
Destroyed completely: not kept by anyone, but handed over wholly to God.
A way of deciding by drawing marked stones or sticks. It was seen as asking for God's will rather than human choice.
Agreeing not to fight each other and to live on good terms.
The share God gave his people to hold and enjoy from generation to generation.
The work someone is given and the position that comes with it.
A large tree of the oak family that bears acorns. Such trees often marked places where important things happened.
A holy place for worshiping God.
God's holy anger against sin.
God's love and mercy that hold on to his people and never change.
Bowing down to honor God.
